1PI3xfMiUE4:39.text: The threat was ...Bd6, skewering the queen with mate to follow — so h3 must come at once, blunting it; if Black tries ...Bd6 anyway, you simply take the bishop on g4.

1PI3xfMiUE4:2.text: Today is a defensive lesson — you're going to sacrifice a knight on purpose and show how to fight on when down material.

1PI3xfMiUE4:5.text: You develop the knight to c3, a Three Knights setup.

1PI3xfMiUE4:6.text: Black develops the bishop to c5. Your plan: sacrifice the knight — but not just yet.

1PI3xfMiUE4:7.text: You develop the bishop to c4.

1PI3xfMiUE4:9.text: Here's the sacrifice — the knight takes on e5, giving up the piece for at least a pawn.

1PI3xfMiUE4:10.text: Black recaptures, dxe5. Objectively you're a piece down and lost — but development isn't finished, so the plan is to complete it and make Black work for the win.

1PI3xfMiUE4:11.text: You play d3, part of finishing development — castle next, then start thinking in earnest.

1PI3xfMiUE4:12.text: Black plays the queen to f6, going for mate — and honestly that's encouraging: this walks into your hands.

1PI3xfMiUE4:13.text: You castle, defending f2. The trouble with the queen on f6 is that it invites a later knight to d5.

1PI3xfMiUE4:14.text: Black guards the square with the knight to e7. Now, the best defensive moves both improve your position and set a trap. The bishop to e3 is logical — if Black trades, you retake with the f-pawn and hit f7 from two sources. But there's something sharper: after the bishop to b3, Black plays ...Bb6 and comes to regret it.

1PI3xfMiUE4:15.text: You want f4 to prise open the f-file for chances — so first the king steps to h1, the classic preparation.

1PI3xfMiUE4:16.text: Black castles, and you're ready for f4.

1PI3xfMiUE4:17.text: You push f4, opening the file and stirring real intrigue on the kingside — the first progress in your counterplay.

1PI3xfMiUE4:19.text: You must recapture with the bishop. Taking with the rook tempts you — it hits the queen — but attacking the queen isn't automatically good: the rook on f4 would be badly placed.

1PI3xfMiUE4:20.text: Black plays the queen to g6. Remember you're only a piece down — win three pawns for it and material is level.

1PI3xfMiUE4:21.text: So you take on c7 with the bishop, snapping off a pawn — pawns like that don't lie by the roadside.

1PI3xfMiUE4:22.text: Black pins with the bishop to g4. You must move the queen — to d2, or the interesting e1 to drag it toward the kingside.

1PI3xfMiUE4:23.text: The queen goes to d2. I avoid e1 because it runs into the knight rerouting to d4, and you want c2 guarded; from d2 the queen can also swing to f4 later.

1PI3xfMiUE4:24.text: Black jumps the knight to d4 — but it no longer carries a threat and hands you a free tempo.

1PI3xfMiUE4:25.text: You play the cryptic bishop to e5, pressing the knight on d4 — hoping Black obliges with the knight from e7 to c6.

1PI3xfMiUE4:26.text: Black finds the queen to h5 instead — a different, even stronger way of hitting your e5-bishop.

1PI3xfMiUE4:27.text: You drop the bishop back to g3 — where it was headed anyway, off the awkward c7-square and out of tactical trouble.

1PI3xfMiUE4:32.text: Black plays the knight to g6. My trick failed — yet it half-worked, because moving that knight has the same effect I was after.

1PI3xfMiUE4:33.text: Here's why I wanted that knight off e7: it guarded d5. Now you plant the knight on d5 and start building central pressure.

1PI3xfMiUE4:34.text: You were eyeing c3 next — but Black finds the knight to e2, a really nasty shot I missed. The bishop to f2 would defend, but ...Bd6 keeps the pressure; your emergency resource is the queen to e1.

1PI3xfMiUE4:35.text: So the queen to e1, forced — Black is playing superbly; that knight leap completely escaped me.

1PI3xfMiUE4:37.text: The knight takes on g3 with check — it was a mating threat — and you recapture with the queen. The trade actually helps you: Black has thinned their own attack, and now h3 is coming.

1PI3xfMiUE4:38.text: Black brings a rook to d8, setting a threat. You have two pawns for the piece — consolidate and you hold real chances.

38QzSkFRn4E:8.text: With d6, Nf6, and the trades on d4 you've steered into a Najdorf — the most theory-heavy of the Sicilians.

38QzSkFRn4E:10.text: The key conceptual split in the Najdorf: category one pushes the pawn two squares with e5, category two plays it only one square to e6. Which you choose depends on what White commits to first.

38QzSkFRn4E:11.text: White's Nf3 retreat is a sideline — it withdraws the knight from the centre, so it isn't testing, but it does ask you how you want to arrange your pieces.

38QzSkFRn4E:12.text: You don't need to commit the e-pawn yet, so just develop — Nc6 — and wait for White to declare themselves.

38QzSkFRn4E:13.text: e5 here simply hands over a pawn without real compensation.

38QzSkFRn4E:14.text: You take with Nxe5, inviting the further trade — because even though the queens come off and you lose castling rights, White can't exploit it.

38QzSkFRn4E:18.text: The king recaptures and looks exposed, but two things save you: White is poorly developed, and the king has a ready-made home. It can simply walk to c7.

38QzSkFRn4E:19.text: Now the point of a6 shines: it covers b5 while the f6-knight covers d5, so together they seal the light squares around the king's future home on c7. First, though, you must be ready to defend the e5-pawn once White castles and swings a rook to e1.

38QzSkFRn4E:20.text: Order matters: e6 first, because it opens the path for the bishop to d6, which will shield the e5-pawn against Rook-e1 pressure.

38QzSkFRn4E:22.text: Kc7 parks the king on its ideal, unassailable square. Now a rook to e1 is comfortably met by Bd6.

38QzSkFRn4E:24.text: White's f4 hopes you take, so they can come out with a bishop-check and spoil things on c7. Instead you trade on your own terms: Bd6 invites White to take on e5 rather than the other way around.

38QzSkFRn4E:26.text: After the recapture the bishop sits beautifully in the centre, and every further trade helps you since you're the one up a pawn.

38QzSkFRn4E:27.text: Ne4 looks scary because Nxe4 runs into the zwischenzug Bxf7-check before White recaptures on e4. But ask the real question — does White actually threaten anything right now? They don't, so you just carry on developing.

38QzSkFRn4E:28.text: So Bd7, the only clean developing move, connecting the rooks — the bishop can always reach the long diagonal later via c6.

38QzSkFRn4E:30.text: Recapturing with the pawn, gxf6, over keeping the structure pretty — the open g-file is worth more here.

38QzSkFRn4E:31.text: The idea behind gxf6 is a slow endgame attack: the g-file plus the light bishop rerouting to c6 build a lasting threat against the g2-pawn — not mate, but relentless pressure.

38QzSkFRn4E:32.text: No rush — Bc6 first. If White tries Bf4, it doesn't work: you take and push f5.

38QzSkFRn4E:36.text: This is the Scandinavian/Caro-Kann pawn formation, and it's far better than it looks because every pawn defends the next. Its one real drawback is that the h7-pawn is isolated.

38QzSkFRn4E:38.text: Activate the rooks starting with Rad8. With only one open file on the board, seizing it usually converts straight into material.

38QzSkFRn4E:43.text: A neat endgame subtlety: the natural doubling with Rg8 and Rg2 fails to Rh4, which guards the h2-pawn and keeps the king safe — so don't rush the second rook to the seventh.

38QzSkFRn4E:44.text: Why allow any counterplay when you can just snap off on b2 instead? There is no need to force the second rook in.

38QzSkFRn4E:46.text: Under checks, tuck the king to b8 — in this endgame the rooks do the work, not the king, so keep it out of the checking lanes.

38QzSkFRn4E:52.text: Simplest is to trade one pair of rooks and immediately plant the other on the open file, hitting the weak queenside pawns.

38QzSkFRn4E:56.text: To win the b4-pawn by force, attack it from behind: Rd4 lets Rb1 defend, but starting with a check and swinging to b2 pins it down — a pawn attacked from behind can't be defended.

38QzSkFRn4E:61.text: Rely on calculation, not vague technique: use the central-kingside pawn majority to deflect White's rook off the back rank, then collect the a-pawn and make new passers.

38QzSkFRn4E:64.text: The best way to defend a pawn is with another pawn — f6 props up the chain rather than tying a rook to defense.

38QzSkFRn4E:68.text: A Russian-school endgame idea worth filing away: pin the pawn laterally along the rank, then bring up your own pawn to win the f3-pawn — commonly missed even at a high level.

38QzSkFRn4E:74.text: This looks like a deep-freeze where one pawn holds two, but it isn't — b6 is a breakthrough. After axb6, the a-pawn runs; it's a sacrifice that costs you nothing.

38QzSkFRn4E:78.text: In the queen-versus-pawn finish, win by zugzwang: force White to shove the h-pawn into a lost race. Kb7 is the elegant key — it makes White dig their own grave.

4T9-0D4SnMk:2.text: White opens with the pawn to d4 and you answer with the knight to f6.

4T9-0D4SnMk:4.text: You play the pawn to g6 — your response doesn't change, a King's Indian setup.

4T9-0D4SnMk:6.text: The bishop to g7, the fianchetto.

4T9-0D4SnMk:7.text: White develops the knight to f3.

4T9-0D4SnMk:8.text: You castle — the kingside is developed, and now you get down to punishing White's overextension in the centre.

4T9-0D4SnMk:9.text: White plays the bishop to e3 — a slightly odd move that locks in the f1-bishop. White's c4-and-d5 chain aims to cramp you, so you want to break it.

4T9-0D4SnMk:10.text: The main point of c6 is that it opens a nice avenue for your queen.

4T9-0D4SnMk:11.text: And if White captures on c6, you'd recapture a pawn while developing a piece. The knight to d2 simply blundered a pawn — you just take.

4T9-0D4SnMk:13.text: After your capture on d5, White brings the queen to c2.

4T9-0D4SnMk:14.text: You keep developing with the knight to c6.

4T9-0D4SnMk:15.text: White plays the knight to d4, offering a trade. The default from beginner level on is to keep the tension — only trade with a good reason — and here I dislike taking, because it lets White's bishop reposition to contest yours and ease their kingside development.

4T9-0D4SnMk:17.text: The knight to d4 threatened nothing, so you developed with d6, and White reroutes the knight to b3. Now aim at the centre, where White's pawn structure is failing.

4T9-0D4SnMk:18.text: You take on d4 first — modifying the move order so White can't reply with a knight capture on c6 that gains a tempo for the defence.

4T9-0D4SnMk:20.text: White recaptures on d4, and you play the pawn to e5.

4T9-0D4SnMk:21.text: White's bishop is chased back to e3 — then the pawn to d4 drives in a nasty wedge.

4T9-0D4SnMk:22.text: But before that, you throw in the bishop to f5 with tempo — not playing automatically; this move has zero downside and a major upside.

4T9-0D4SnMk:23.text: White plays the queen to d2, and now you don't play d4 at all, since it might allow the bishop to h6.

4T9-0D4SnMk:24.text: Instead you take on c4 — far more efficient, winning another pawn, and White is suffocating without any kingside development.

4T9-0D4SnMk:25.text: White plays the knight to a5. It hangs by a single thread — if you could kick the queen off the diagonal you'd win it, but the knight to e4 runs into the queen to b4, a dead end. So look at the interference tactic.

4T9-0D4SnMk:26.text: The pawn to c3 — the interference tactic. It's a deep move: after the queen takes it, you hunt the knight and induce further concessions.

4T9-0D4SnMk:28.text: The knight to d5 — hitting the queen and preparing to cash in. If the queen drops back, you take the bishop and White can't recapture with the queen.

4T9-0D4SnMk:29.text: Not the best way to win, but one of several.

DO28z1MTaC8:32.text: The rook takes, capturing on f5.

DO28z1MTaC8:33.text: The rook to g2 — this seems like capitulation of their attack, which I like; it means they don't know what to do and is milking my clock. Now g7 is protected; you want to triple, with the knight to d4 and the rook to f8 coming.

DO28z1MTaC8:34.text: The rook to f8, continuing to pile pieces on the kingside — no need to change strategy.

DO28z1MTaC8:35.text: They take, capturing on b6 — you have to take.

DO28z1MTaC8:36.text: You recapture, capturing on b6, checking for intermediate moves first — nothing there.

DO28z1MTaC8:37.text: The bishop to e6 — a very advanced idea I'll admit I missed: if you move the rook, they play the bishop to g4 and wins a piece. So you'll have to sac the exchange.

DO28z1MTaC8:38.text: You sac the exchange with the knight to e7.

DO28z1MTaC8:40.text: After the bishop takes f5 and you recapture with the knight on f5, my worry isn't even the position, it's the clock.

DO28z1MTaC8:41.text: I always check the game afterward — they're playing very well, but I've seen 1800s play this well many times.

DO28z1MTaC8:43.text: ...then the knight to f3 recaptures their queen, winning back the exchange, and you're up a pawn.

DO28z1MTaC8:44.text: A very hard endgame to win with one minute, but I'll try my best.

DO28z1MTaC8:46.text: They take on g4, and the knight to f3 comes with check.

DO28z1MTaC8:48.text: The king to g2, and the knight takes, capturing on d2.

DO28z1MTaC8:49.text: They recapture with the bishop on d2.

DO28z1MTaC8:50.text: You play the knight to f4, check, centralizing it; if they take, that's a good trade for you — up a pawn.

DO28z1MTaC8:52.text: You recapture, capturing on f4 — a very nice rook on f4, and you're up a pawn.

DO28z1MTaC8:54.text: Let's get your king out — the king to g8.

DCBwXvH3kH4:2.text: The Queen's Gambit — you offer the c-pawn to deflect Black's center.

DCBwXvH3kH4:4.text: The knight to f6 is the Marshall Defense — a cross between a Grünfeld and a Queen's Gambit Declined that simply doesn't work, though White must be precise to prove it.

DCBwXvH3kH4:6.text: You take on d5 and Black recaptures with the knight, exactly as the Marshall intends.

DCBwXvH3kH4:7.text: The strongest reply is e4, kicking the knight and grabbing a broad pawn center at once.

DCBwXvH3kH4:9.text: Now the move you have to know: the bishop to d3. It looks quiet, but the natural knight to c3 is actually a mistake — it walks into e5, when the queen trade with check leaves White scrambling. Bishop to d3 sidesteps all of it and keeps the edge.

DCBwXvH3kH4:11.text: You develop circumspectly with h3, so a bishop to g4 can always be met by f3 — a small luxury you can afford because Black burned tempi shuffling the knight around.

DCBwXvH3kH4:19.text: Rather than the passive bishop to e3, you go to g5 — the pawn on d4 is already held by the knight, so you spend the bishop on pressure instead of defense.

DCBwXvH3kH4:21.text: The simplest plan: go after the fianchetto bishop. The queen to d2 prepares the bishop to h6 — trade that bishop and Black's king weakens and their grip on d4 loosens.

DCBwXvH3kH4:23.text: When Black lunges with c5 you don't take — that would justify their whole setup. You push d5, jamming the door shut and keeping a protected passer.

DCBwXvH3kH4:26.text: Black recaptures on e5, and note the risk in that: once a fianchettoed bishop ventures off g7, it can struggle to get home, leaving holes and inviting f4.

DCBwXvH3kH4:27.text: So the bishop to h6 makes them regret it, cutting the bishop off from its return square.

DCBwXvH3kH4:29.text: There's no rush and no reason to wait — you take on g7 and strip the king's defender.

DCBwXvH3kH4:31.text: The rook belongs on d1: if Black frees themselves with e6 and the pawns come off, that rook stacks behind the queen down the d-file.

DCBwXvH3kH4:33.text: The knight to e2 does double duty — it stops b5 indirectly and reroutes toward the kingside, since it was only biting on granite where it stood.

DCBwXvH3kH4:35.text: On to g3, bringing the knight into the coming kingside assault.

DCBwXvH3kH4:37.text: Now the gas pedal: f4. You prepared slowly, and this is where you attack fast.

DCBwXvH3kH4:39.text: The finish begins with the queen check on c3, driving the king back before the combination.

DCBwXvH3kH4:41.text: You crack it open by taking on e6 — Black's passive position simply can't hold everything together.

DCBwXvH3kH4:43.text: After the recapture the bishop swings to c4, joining the pile-up on the e6 weakness.

DCBwXvH3kH4:45.text: Then f5 lands with tremendous force — the whole position collapses.

DCBwXvH3kH4:47.text: The bishop takes on e6 with check, ripping the king open.

DCBwXvH3kH4:49.text: Here's the crusher — the knight is pinned, and with king and queen lined up on the same rank the rook check on d7 wins outright.

DCBwXvH3kH4:51.text: You collect the queen and the wheels come off.

DCBwXvH3kH4:14.text: Why the natural knight to c3 fails here: after e5, taking with the pawn drops into a queen trade with check, and the knight jump to g4 forks with the extra pawn regained — White ends up worse.

DCBwXvH3kH4:13.text: The other sound try is the knight to f3; after the exchange on d4 and the queen recapture White keeps a small endgame pull — though many players won't want an endgame that early, which is why d3 is the most accurate.

DO28z1MTaC8:62.text: The king to g6 — I want to make things go boom on the other side of the board.

DO28z1MTaC8:69.text: They offer a rook trade with the rook to e4 — if this is a draw I'll be shocked; let me calculate.

DO28z1MTaC8:70.text: Let's take it — the rook capturing on e4.

DO28z1MTaC8:74.text: The king to h4, and you play g6.

DO28z1MTaC8:78.text: The king to g3, and you push d5.

DO28z1MTaC8:82.text: The king to e2, and you push h4 — this is winning: two passed pawns.

DO28z1MTaC8:83.text: They take, capturing on d4 — but I've plenty of clock; this is not a draw.

DO28z1MTaC8:84.text: You recapture, capturing on d4 — two connected passers too far from their king.

DO28z1MTaC8:88.text: You push d3 — d2, d1, and it's a queen. There's no stalemate: I leave them a pawn, then walk my king around to mate on the other side. A tip: when mating with a couple of seconds left, leave your opponent pawn moves so you never have to worry about stalemate.

DO28z1MTaC8:3.text: The knight to f3 — I'd love to play the Elephant Gambit or the Stafford here.

DO28z1MTaC8:4.text: You play the knight to f6, angling for the Stafford.

DO28z1MTaC8:5.text: But the knight to c3 sidesteps it — no Stafford now. You can play d5 here for an interesting game, and the bishop to c5 might transpose to the Stafford.

DO28z1MTaC8:6.text: You try the bishop to c5, Eric Rosen style, hoping to goad a gambit.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:2.text: Your Sicilian again — you'll test the Accelerated Dragon at this level.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:5.text: White plays the Alapin, the pawn to c3 — building a big center behind d4 rather than opening the main lines.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:6.text: Here I'll show a practical, lesser-known try: the immediate d5, striking the center before White is ready.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:7.text: White pushes e5, trying to move-order you into a French Advance. The escape is that your light-squared bishop isn't shut in yet — you can develop it outside the pawn chain first and reach an improved French.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:8.text: The bishop to g4 is the ambitious choice — it pins the knight and leans on the center, challenging White the most. Then e6 gives you a French on steroids, bishop already outside the chain.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:9.text: The line I wanted to show against the Alapin: after d5, meet it with d4. Then the exchanges on d4 and the break e5 give Black a fully sound game.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:10.text: So the queen to c7 — less exposed than b6, and it leans on the e5-pawn, so you're happy to recapture there if White trades on c6.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:12.text: And that's the point — you take back with the queen, keeping the structure intact and a fine position.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:13.text: White plays d4 and you've reached exactly that improved French. Rather than a sharp tactical fling that leaves your king behind, you'll keep it simple.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:14.text: The clean e6 — an intuitive judgment call, no need for tricks when you have a healthy, easy position.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:18.text: The Caro-Kann-style route pays off: the knight goes to f5 via e7, pressuring the d4-pawn from its ideal square.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:24.text: c4 closes the queenside and makes White's rook lift look pointless — a psychologically awkward move to face, even if it eases the pressure on d4.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:28.text: An unconventional idea — the capture on a4, opening the b-file. Normally you'd never crack open the queenside like this, but White is so passive that the open file is all yours, and that a-pawn is now a weakness.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:30.text: Now you finish development and castle — no need for a defensive a5; White has nothing scary there.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:34.text: Back to the strong idea: the bishop to a3, which does several things at once and, if the rook steps to a1, drops to b2 with a fork.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:41.text: After the trade on f3 White's structure is shattered — and, just as important, the recapture removed a defender of the d4-pawn, which now has two attackers and two defenders and can't survive one more.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:42.text: Rooks before queens: the rook to b3 is the classy, doubt-free move — you may not even need to win d4, just triple down the b-file and let the problems solve themselves.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:44.text: You double with the rook to b8, and the threat of crashing in on b1 becomes decisive — the knight has done its job and hands the game to the rooks.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:46.text: The finale opens with the knight check on h4, and the mating net closes.

Dj_hLEdDpAg:16.text: After the queens come off, the bishop to g4 gives Black obvious, strong compensation for the pawn — White's king is stuck in the center while Black is ready to castle long and win the pawn back.

DO28z1MTaC8:2.text: You answer e4 with e5, looking for something offbeat.

DO28z1MTaC8:9.text: White castles. Now, to make it hard for them to develop, how do you add some spice?

DO28z1MTaC8:10.text: The bishop to g4 — because if you play the knight to c6 first, knowing their style they'll play h3 and you'll regret it, so you squeeze this in while you can. They'll probably retreat to e2.

DO28z1MTaC8:12.text: Now you play the knight to c6, threatening the knight to d4.

DO28z1MTaC8:13.text: The bishop to e3. A classic line. The knight to d4 is possible but less strong with the bishop on e3, since they can take with the bishop and keep their structure. Against boring players, keep the tension — give them rope and force decisions.

DO28z1MTaC8:14.text: The classic way to make White decide is to drop the bishop back to b6, avoiding their taking on c5 and ruining your structure — and if they take now, a takes b6 gives you doubled pawns that don't matter, plus the a-file, which is great.

DO28z1MTaC8:15.text: Make these players think, and they'll do something irrational or panic. h3.

DO28z1MTaC8:16.text: You drop the bishop to h5 — they'll probably contemplate g4 for a while; if they play it, you consider a sacrifice on g4.

DO28z1MTaC8:17.text: I don't think the time's right for the sac — not enough there — so you keep the bishop. They play the king to h2, a weird move; maybe planning the rook to g1 and g4.

DO28z1MTaC8:18.text: You just castle — no point doing anything wild.

DO28z1MTaC8:19.text: The queen to d2. Now I see their idea: the king went to h2 so that after the bishop takes f3, g takes f3 keeps their king off the open file, and they can play the rook to g1 and attack down the g-file — even with a ruined structure, they get the file.

DO28z1MTaC8:20.text: Does that warrant not taking on f3? No — the bishop takes f3, capturing on f3, creates such damage on their kingside that it's worth it, as long as you're careful.

DO28z1MTaC8:21.text: They recapture, capturing on f3. The weaknesses they've created are permanent, so it's worth it if you manage the open g-file. Two things: start kingside operations, moves like the knight to h5, and balance that with some prophylaxis.

DO28z1MTaC8:22.text: The greater priority is to stake a claim on the kingside so they don't run circles over you — so the knight to h5, getting the wheels turning.

DO28z1MTaC8:23.text: The rook to g1 — a pin. Many people reflexively play the king to h8, but that tempo could matter against a skilled attacker. Where's the queen doing more, on f6 or h4? Only one creates a threat.

DO28z1MTaC8:24.text: The queen to f6 — on h4 it does nothing, since you've no light-squared bishop to hit h3; on f6 it's active.

DO28z1MTaC8:25.text: The rook to g4, ignoring the attack on f3 — this guy's legit, gone from passive to aggressive in a snap.

DO28z1MTaC8:26.text: As the Russian expression goes, having said A you must say B — putting the queen on f6 and NOT taking on f3 makes no sense, so the queen takes f3, capturing on f3.

DO28z1MTaC8:27.text: The rook to g1, doubling — now the threats on g7 are serious. One more move and they create insurmountable threats, probably a sacrifice; g6 doesn't solve it, and they could sack on g6 via the pin. So now's the time.

DO28z1MTaC8:28.text: The king to h8 — the problem is the g-file, not their bishop. The king to h8 is the better move.

DO28z1MTaC8:29.text: The knight to d5 is good — this guy's very legit. You keep attacking; your king is very safe.

DO28z1MTaC8:30.text: You need spice on the kingside — open files, something to join this lonely queen. So f5 — gutsy play by both sides.

DO28z1MTaC8:31.text: They take, capturing on f5. With my queen so dominant and the knight on h5 defending g7, I'm optimistic about the attack.

IMBSR0A9nJs:32.text: Black tries the resilient king to e7 — but they're cooked. A general rule: while the king sits on its home square, never assume you must defend along the e-file, because of the pin.

IMBSR0A9nJs:34.text: And again on e5 — the e-file pin doing the work.

IMBSR0A9nJs:35.text: The rook takes on e5 with check. No need to rush your development — there's nothing Black can do, so you take your time and mop up.

IMBSR0A9nJs:36.text: Black plays the king to f7. The fastest way to win is to go after the king — the bishop to d5 is the natural route.

IMBSR0A9nJs:38.text: The bishop to d5 with check forces the king back — if it steps to f6, the rook swoops to e8 and wins more.

IMBSR0A9nJs:39.text: The rook to e8 — and now it's totally over.

IMBSR0A9nJs:40.text: Black plays the bishop to d7.

IMBSR0A9nJs:41.text: The rook takes on g8 — not the other capture, which would hang your rook — and you're up an enormous amount of material.

IMBSR0A9nJs:43.text: This forces the rook trade, and the rest is simple, up a rook and a piece. What matters isn't the individual move but adhering to the correct general strategy.

IMBSR0A9nJs:5.text: I like the Italian-flavoured approach — the bishop to c4 — and only later d4. It's flexible: you can also play the pawn to d3 and transpose to an Italian structure if you prefer.

IMBSR0A9nJs:6.text: Black plays the pawn to c6 — not prioritizing development.

IMBSR0A9nJs:7.text: So it's natural to open the centre with the pawn to d4. You could castle first, but there's no reason to delay — the time has come to open the centre.

IMBSR0A9nJs:11.text: So the knight recaptures on d4, centralizing. Black looks to be aiming for the pawn to c5 — but c5 is bad.

IMBSR0A9nJs:15.text: The bishop captures the rook in the corner — the more-developed side wins the scramble.

IMBSR0A9nJs:16.text: Black plays the queen to b6, a good move defending the d4-pawn. Tempted to rescue your bishop with the bishop to d5, but you don't need to — the d5-square, protected by your pawn, is always available, and the bishop is nearly impossible to attack where it is.

IMBSR0A9nJs:10.text: Black takes on d4 — and you should recapture with the knight, not the queen, since a queen there would be vulnerable to ideas like the pawn to c5.

IMBSR0A9nJs:2.text: You have White, open with the pawn to e4, and get e5 — a reply you haven't faced much this run.

IMBSR0A9nJs:4.text: The bishop belongs on c4 in these positions — the check on b5 makes little sense, since Black can just answer with the pawn to c6.

IMBSR0A9nJs:8.text: Black expands with the pawn to b5 — common at this level and nothing to fear; you've already developed and seized the centre.

IMBSR0A9nJs:9.text: You simply drop the bishop back to b3, staying on the strong diagonal.

IMBSR0A9nJs:12.text: A perfect illustration of what happens when you don't develop: the side with more development tends to prevail in these tactical skirmishes.

IMBSR0A9nJs:13.text: Playing as clinically as possible with the bishop to d5 — you'll end up an exchange and a pawn to the good, which is a lot.

IMBSR0A9nJs:17.text: So castling is the simplest, best approach.

IMBSR0A9nJs:18.text: Black develops the bishop to e7. Two ways to handle the d4-pawn: reroute the knight, to f3 or better b3, to attack it — or transform the advantage with the pawn to c3.

IMBSR0A9nJs:19.text: The pawn to c3 — a classic transformation: you give back the d4-pawn, but in return you get the c3-square for the knight, the e3-square for the bishop, and the open c-file.

IMBSR0A9nJs:20.text: Black plays the knight to a6, heading for c7 — a cute idea but not dangerous. You can simply play the queen takes d4 to steer into a queen trade.

IMBSR0A9nJs:21.text: The queen takes d4 — and it essentially forces the trade, because it also hits the g7-pawn: a fork.

IMBSR0A9nJs:23.text: You recapture with the pawn. The in-between check on c6 was possible, but no need to be fancy — the bishop is perfectly safe.

IMBSR0A9nJs:24.text: Black plays the bishop to f6. You're clearly winning — now capitalize efficiently. If the knight goes to c7, you answer with the bishop to c6.

IMBSR0A9nJs:25.text: Since Black is undeveloped on the kingside, you push the pawn to e5. If Black takes twice, the rook to e1 pins the bishop and the pawn to f4 wins it.

IMBSR0A9nJs:27.text: The classic pin-and-win idea unfolds with the exchange on e5.

IMBSR0A9nJs:29.text: The rook to e1 — and Black walks right into the pin.

IMBSR0A9nJs:30.text: Black tries the pawn to f6 to hold.

IMBSR0A9nJs:31.text: The pawn to f4 — the important motif: the pin plus f4 wins the pinned bishop. Now it's over.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:15.text: On e3 the bishop actually does a great job further supporting the chain, which you want rock-solid. But first, the knight to f3 — let's get the pieces you know how to place out.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:10.text: And I wanted to punish Black concretely for the knight to d7.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:7.text: I rejected a knight to c3 because a capture on e4 and then e5 tends to transpose into more conventional play.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:9.text: And there's a second point to f4 beyond bolstering e5 — it opens the natural developing square for the g1 knight to reach f3.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:13.text: Now f4 — the maximally ambitious, textbook move, grabbing space and taking the fight to the opponent.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:14.text: You could instead play a bishop to e3.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:17.text: So the bishop to e3 — and the subtlety is that when the knight lands on f5, your bishop slides back to f2. Castle first and that retreat to e3 is no longer available; the small developmental detail decides how smoothly the game runs.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:18.text: Your opponent played sensibly for a while — g6 was normal.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:19.text: The knight comes to f5, and the bishop drops to f2, first overprotecting the d4 pawn and, much later, eyeing a route into Black's position.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:20.text: A bishop maneuver to h4 and f6 is a common infiltration, especially against a fianchetto with a bishop fianchettoed to g7.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:21.text: You castle and keep developing. The h5 push is typical for this structure.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:22.text: h5 does prevent g4, but it creates major dark-square weaknesses — notice the outpost on g5. That doesn't mean you leap there now; a knight to g5 lets Black trade and fill the holes. Later, though, g5 becomes a transit square, and a plan of trading on f5 and swinging the bishop to h4 hands your queen a swarm of juicy kingside outposts. With the center closed you have time — the position simply doesn't change fast.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:23.text: A knight to a3 is a dead-end after a6, so instead the b1 knight goes to d2 — toward the center, going nowhere in particular yet, a Frankfurt-airport move you never regret. Remember, closed positions offer two broad plans: arrange your pieces to blast the center open, or maneuver on a flank.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:2.text: You open e4 and meet the Caro-Kann — c6.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:3.text: d4, taking the full center behind the pawn.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:4.text: Black strikes with d5, questioning your e4 pawn head-on.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:5.text: Both previous Fantasy opponents in this speedrun grabbed on e4 and then erred with a knight to f6, an Alapin-Caro crossover. This time it's different.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:6.text: Here you focused on your opponent's new move, since I'd never seen it and wanted to be sure you responded well — and I think you did.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:8.text: Nothing is developed yet, so the chain is your lifeline; c3 keeps it intact.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:11.text: After a capture on e5 the engine says White is a touch better — but how lame to bail into an endgame this fast in the Fantasy?

Jt5bST3j-Cw:12.text: Black plays e6, and you keep everything as flexible as possible — with the opponent playing so unambitiously, you can leave many developing paths open.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:16.text: Black's knight goes to e7, heading for f5 to press d4 in true French fashion. Don't be tempted by g4 to stop it — that's far too cavalier with so little developed. After g4, h5 is a classic response: you can't answer h3, Black captures on g4, and the h1 rook hangs, so g4 hands Black a huge f5 outpost instead of denying one.

Jt5bST3j-Cw:24.text: Black plays a queen to b6. Here's your plan: rip the whole thing open and bank on your more active pieces handling the chaos better. Not a capture on c5 — that just hands Black space and the e3 square. QVw89_6fh2Y:23.text: White steps the king to e2, but it brings little relief. A common mistake is to win a pawn and then rest — dropping back or trading knights — but you have a better way.

QVw89_6fh2Y:24.text: Don't forget your knight is hanging, but you don't want to stop at one pawn while White's position is collapsing. The instinctive move is a knight to b4 — it hits the pawn, pressures the bishop, and sits very stably.

QVw89_6fh2Y:25.text: White is lost. After a rook to c1, you have a really pretty move.

QVw89_6fh2Y:26.text: You might expect a knight capture on d5, but I prefer a capture on a2 — it also hits the rook, and if White takes your queen you recapture with a fork.

QVw89_6fh2Y:28.text: White takes and walks right into it, and you win — up a ton of material.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:30.text: The b-pawn takes c6 — the hanging-pawn structure: pawns on c6 and d5 with no b- or e-pawn, a self-sufficient island. Think of it as the isolated pawn shifting from the d-file to the c-file: c6 is now essentially isolated, since d5 can't go backwards to defend it.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:31.text: A lot of tactics hanging in the air; the fact that they're thinking this long is encouraging.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:28.text: Black's in a little trouble — hard to move, since moving the queen off d8 allows the bishop takes f6, spoiling the structure. The bishop to d7 is a good 2100 move, keeping the tension and protecting the knight. Black threatens the knight takes d4 with tactics, and the bishop takes d7 there loses a piece to the capture on f3. So you can change the nature of your advantage from an IQP to something more dynamic — my instinct is an unnatural move.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:32.text: The queen to e8 was a smart proposal, unpinning and hitting the knight. Black plays c5, which I expected, but it fails tactically to a beautiful sequence I saw when playing the bishop takes c6. Your instinct is to move the knight from d4, but the bishop takes f6 is available — the queen still can't recapture, and the knight takes d7 comes with a fork. After the bishop takes f6, the pawn recaptures, you take the bishop on d7 and claim a small edge on Black's damaged kingside — though they could tuck the king to h8 and use the g-file. There's a specific tactical line, but I need a little more time; there's a detail I missed, which may force me off my intended path.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:33.text: So you resort to the straightforward path — take on f6, take on d7, and claim a small advantage based on the weak hanging pawns and the weak king. The bishop takes f6; you have to play faster given the clock.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:34.text: The queen takes f6 would lose on the spot. The g-pawn recaptures. The knight to c6 here fails tactically to the bishop takes c6, the knight takes c6, and the queen to e8.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:35.text: The knight takes d7 — you either see these tactical details or you don't; a lot of top-level chess boils down to spotting them.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:36.text: The queen recaptures. Now you have to move your knight and figure out where it belongs.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:37.text: The knight to f3 I don't like, because it'd be restricted by the f6-pawn — so the knight to c2, keeping the diagonal open for the queen and able to reroute to e3 to keep harassing the d5-pawn, one of Black's main weaknesses, along with f6. White's better, not as big as I'd hoped, but only one side is having fun. The queen to f3 targets d5 and f6 and defends g2, nipping any g-file pressure in the bud, a good response to the king to h8. On Black's d4: a passed pawn is double-edged, still isolated after the trade, and you take on d4 and play the queen to f3 with tempo. The queen to f5 for Black is an impulsive blunder walking into the knight to e3 fork.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:38.text: I like positions where both sides have only one minor piece — very instructive. It's not really good-knight-versus-bad-bishop, since their bishop activates with c4, but the bigger problem is all the pawn weaknesses and the flimsy king. The rook to d8 makes the king even more uncomfortable; I'd start with the queen to f3, forcing Black to contend with the threat of the queen takes f6. If Black throws in d4 anyway, after the trades I'd seriously consider not taking on f6, since it lets the d-pawn run with d3, but White's still good; the rook to d1 also works. The queen to d6 protects f6, but now the knight reaches f5 with tempo, so the knight to e3 gets even more tempting.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:40.text: The queen to f3, the queen to d6. Both the rook to d1 — the measured Russian-schoolboy approach, later lifting to the kingside via d3 — and the knight to e3 are good; the knight to e3 is super juicy, since the knight to f5 with the queen to g4 and g7 could lead to checkmate very quickly. My guess is the king to h8 in response; you start with the knight to e3. The bishop to c7 is a one-move threat, met simply by g3, keeping the tension — don't give an empty check on g4, which only helps Black reach h8, and definitely don't trade queens.

TvgWwc1dBb8:6.text: Nf6, the Two Knights, is a very practical intermediate choice — the Fried Liver isn't as scary as its reputation, and there's less tricky theory than after Bc5.

TvgWwc1dBb8:7.text: d4 is the Max Lange / Nakhmanson tricky line. You take, exd4, and castle — nothing to fear if you know the ideas.

TvgWwc1dBb8:10.text: Playing principled chess, you grab on e4 into the Max Lange — the tamer d6 keeps it out of theory but leaves the bishop passive on e7.

TvgWwc1dBb8:12.text: The knight is attacked, so d5 defends it, and for a moment Black looks two pawns up and dominant — but this is the Max Lange, and it's all theory.

TvgWwc1dBb8:15.text: The century-old point: Nc3 can't be taken — the knight is pinned, and capturing with the pawn drops the queen — so the queen must move, and White recaptures with heavy e-file pressure. The whole line is objectively equal.

TvgWwc1dBb8:16.text: Qh5 is a safe square and x-rays the knight on f3 — never a bad thing in these positions.

TvgWwc1dBb8:18.text: The calculation that decides it: after a queen trade, the d4-knight would be guarded only by the rook on e4 — and rooks and queens are terrible defenders, being so easy to chase. So Be7, then f5 shoves the rook along the fourth rank and g5 again, until White must give up the exchange.

TvgWwc1dBb8:20.text: Qd5 centralizes the queen, hits the rook, and adds a second defender to d4 all at once.

TvgWwc1dBb8:24.text: d3 is the star — a strong passed pawn deep in White's camp. Even if they win it back, the tempi and energy they burn doing so let you pour your other pieces into the game. It's win-win.

TvgWwc1dBb8:30.text: Now the positional queen sacrifice: Qxe4, giving the queen for a rook and a piece. It's not a two-move tactic — it's a judgment. The d3-pawn is so strong, and White so passive, that the pieces and the pawn will outweigh the queen. After a sac like this, there's no need to hurry.

TvgWwc1dBb8:36.text: Improve calmly — the bishop to the long diagonal — because with a rook, knight, and bishop for the queen you have time on your side.

TvgWwc1dBb8:38.text: Bxf3 wrecks White's structure and opens the d4 square for the knight — though the immediate Nd4 would be a blunder to Qxd3, so stay patient.

TvgWwc1dBb8:40.text: Re8 seizes the freshly opened file, beating White to it — if they try Rd1 you trade and strip the defenders away from your d-pawn.

TvgWwc1dBb8:44.text: d2 marches the pawn a step from queening. But find the order — Re1-check at once just lets the king run to g2, so first crank the pieces to maximum, centralize the knight, and only then break through.

TNaKFN65B5o:44.text: You recapture, and the f-file is yours with a million threats — a rook to f2 hitting the queen and threatening mate on g2. Q0CTfDwnd3A:2.text: The pawn to e4, c5 — the Alapin.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:3.text: e6 is one of many moves a tier behind the two mains, d5 and the knight to f6 —

Q0CTfDwnd3A:4.text: — a flexible move in which Black can play several different ways.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:6.text: The traditional response is d5. To play it, Black has to be okay allowing e5, an Advanced French — but since I don't play the Advanced and never have, most Sicilian players are really bluffing White into e5, and often neither side knows what to do.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:7.text: The more Alapin-esque way is to take on d5, and Black is at an early crossroads: recapture with the queen, transposing, or keep the e6 spirit with the pawn — and you can already see the IQP structure forming.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:8.text: If Black recaptures with the pawn and White later takes on c5, Black recaptures and has an isolated pawn on d5 — the classic isolated queen's pawn. One good thing about c3: after you take on c5 and they recapture, that c3-pawn slows the d5-pawn and controls the square in front of it, the most important thing against the IQP — controlling the square matters more than occupying it. Taking on c5 immediately is decent but not best; ideally, as in the Queen's Gambit, you wait for Black to move the dark-squared bishop first, then take on c5 to cost them a tempo.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:9.text: The bishop to d7 is a move, but generally trades favor the side fighting the IQP, since the fewer pieces, the harder it is to hold or control that pawn —

Q0CTfDwnd3A:10.text: — the knight to c6 is the more topical response. Now you follow the rule and don't take on c5 yet.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:11.text: Instead you develop and wait for a more opportune moment — the moment Black develops their bishop is a very good time to take on c5. The knight to f3.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:12.text: The bishop to d6 — funnily, you can delay the pawn takes c5 one more move by castling, since Black can't resolve the central tension, but I'll stick to the traditional way.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:13.text: Traditionally you take on c5 the moment Black develops their bishop —

Q0CTfDwnd3A:14.text: — the bishop takes c5, and you've earned a tempo, since Black made an extra move with their bishop.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:15.text: Now you castle and get your king out of the centre. The next big question is where Black develops their knight — e7 or f6. Against the knight to f6, I like the bishop to g5, pinning it; but if the knight goes to e7, the bishop to g5 makes less sense.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:16.text: The knight to f6 — the bishop to g5 walks into f6, and here f6 isn't so weakening you'd want to spend tempi inducing it. Important IQP ideas: the check on e1 is tempting, but Black covers with the bishop and the f2-pawn becomes a major problem — the queen to b6, or the bishop takes f2 forking king and bishop — so keep the rook on f1 to solidify f2. Two questions: where the bishop goes, which is g5, and what to do with the knight — in these structures the knight often goes to b3, hits the bishop, and heads for the blockade square.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:17.text: There really aren't other options for the knight; the real decision is the order. I like starting with the bishop to g5, restricting the knight and immediately setting up a pin.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:18.text: The bishop to e6. The drawback of playing the knight to d2 first —

Q0CTfDwnd3A:20.text: — is that the bishop would be temporarily blocked in by the knight.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:22.text: So this seems a more harmonious way of developing. The bishop to e6 follows — I don't love it; Black delays castling, giving you options like the immediate knight to e4, pressuring their minor pieces —

Q0CTfDwnd3A:23.text: — but I don't want too many adventurous moves; I want to play traditionally to highlight your IQP technique. The knight to d2. White is slightly better — not because Black has an IQP, since you can't make categorical assertions about the isolated queen's pawn; it depends on the placement of the other pieces.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:24.text: This resembles the bad-IQP case more than the good, because Black's piece activity isn't impressive — he's pinned along the diagonal, and the bishop on e6 is a passive observer tied to the pawn.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:25.text: And as you play the knight to b3, you achieve complete control of the square in front of the pawn —

Q0CTfDwnd3A:26.text: — so the IQP is no longer a moving target; it'll saddle Black for as long as it sits on d5. Now you make marginal improving moves. Avoid the queen to d2, which runs into the knight to e4 and bad trades. The low-hanging fruit is a knight to d4 — controlling the square matters most, but occupying it isn't bad either; the knight to c4 is also on an ideal square, pressuring their minors.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:27.text: The knight to d4 — I prefer the knight from b3, keeping the other knight on the kingside where it supports your king. Now you threaten to win a pawn by taking twice on c6; if the knight takes d4, you recapture with the knight.

Q0CTfDwnd3A:29.text: The bishop takes c6 — it transforms your advantage from a strictly positional one into an actual initiative based on superior piece activity. Two minuses: you give up the bishop pair, and, more importantly, you allow the b-pawn recapture, after which the d5-pawn is no longer isolated.

_zT8aWZh2x0:17.text: The bishop takes on f3 and White recaptures with the bishop — Black cashes in the pin, trading off a key defender of the light squares.

_zT8aWZh2x0:19.text: The knight swings to e5, the classic King's Indian outpost, and White retreats the bishop to e2 to keep it. A beautiful square: central, secure, hard to dislodge.

_zT8aWZh2x0:28.text: The rook comes to c8, onto the half-open c-file — the natural home for a King's Indian rook once the c-file opens.
